title: Quark: What It Is, How Much Protein It Has, and How It Differs From Skyr and Cottage Cheese

seo.title: Quark: Protein, Texture, and How It Differs From Skyr and Cottage
seo.meta_description: Quark is a smooth, mildly tangy fresh cheese. Lower-fat versions often provide roughly 10–13 g protein per 100 g. Compare its process, texture, fat, and protein with skyr and cottage cheese.
seo.search_intent: Understand what quark is, how it is made, how much protein it contains, and how it differs from skyr and cottage cheese in texture, composition, and processing.

excerpt: Quark is a fresh, mainly acid-set cheese with a smooth texture and mild tang. Protein varies by formulation: studies of quark-type cheeses place many versions around 10–13 g per 100 g. It can resemble skyr in thickness and protein density, but it is not the same product; compared with cottage cheese, quark is much smoother and lacks visible curds.
content_html:
Quark is a fresh, mildly tangy cheese made by acidifying milk so the casein coagulates, then removing part of the whey. It is not aged, so it retains far more moisture than a ripened cheese and usually has a smooth, spoonable texture.

That appearance puts it in the same mental category as skyr, thick yogurt, and cottage cheese. The resemblance is useful, but texture alone can be misleading: three white high-protein dairy foods can be made by quite different processes.

How much protein does quark contain?

The answer depends heavily on moisture and fat. In a study of cow's-milk quark-type cheeses, full-fat versions averaged about 10.3 g protein per 100 g while reduced-fat versions averaged about 12.8 g/100 g. The Canadian Dairy Commission lists a typical skim-milk quark at about 12 g/100 g.

That places many quarks firmly in the high-protein range for fresh dairy, but commercial labels can vary. More whey removal concentrates milk solids, while higher moisture or fat changes the percentage of protein in the finished cheese.

A 150-g serving of quark containing 12 g protein per 100 g would provide about 18 g of protein. That serving-level number is often more useful than comparing percentages in isolation.

Why is quark so smooth?

Quark is formed primarily through acid coagulation of milk proteins, followed by drainage. Heat treatment, homogenization, fat level, and how aggressively the curd is drained all influence moisture retention, firmness, and protein concentration.

Unlike cottage cheese, the goal is not to preserve large individual curds. The finished product is usually uniform and creamy rather than visibly lumpy.

Quark can also retain a meaningful amount of lactose because it is a moist fresh cheese and its curd is not washed in the classic cottage-cheese manner. That can matter for people with lactose intolerance.

Quark vs. skyr: similar bowls, different traditions and processing

Modern skyr is typically sold as a very thick, high-protein cultured dairy food. One digestion study used a skyr containing about 10% protein, which clearly overlaps with many quark products.

Protein alone therefore does not separate them. Skyr relies on fermentation and substantial concentration, while quark is traditionally classified as a fresh acid-set cheese. Depending on the manufacturer, both can be very low in fat and equally smooth.

It is not accurate to say that one always has more protein. Two brands can easily reverse the comparison, so the actual nutrition label matters more than the category name.

Quark vs. cottage cheese: curd structure is the easiest distinction

Cottage cheese is also a fresh cheese, but its curd is handled differently. The curd is cut into distinct pieces, may be cooked and washed, and is often mixed with a cream dressing. The finished product therefore retains visible curds and a grainier bite.

A 2025 review places cottage cheese at roughly 11–13.8 g protein per 100 g, and Canadian Dairy Commission reference values include about 12.5–14 g/100 g for common creamed or lower-fat styles. That range overlaps substantially with quark.

Cottage cheese is also commonly saltier because salt is an important part of its formulation. Quark is often milder and less salty, although recipes vary by country and brand.

Which one makes sense depends on texture, label, and use

Quark works especially well when you want a smooth base for breakfast bowls, sauces, fillings, or baking. Cottage cheese contributes visible curd texture and often fits savory meals. Skyr commonly functions more like a very thick spoonable cultured dairy snack.

Nutritionally, all three can be excellent sources of dairy protein. The meaningful differences often come down to fat, sodium, residual lactose, added ingredients, and protein density in the product you actually buy.

The practical rule: think of quark as a smooth fresh acid-set cheese, not another name for skyr or cottage cheese. If protein is your priority, compare grams per 100 g and per serving. If texture or cooking behavior matters, the manufacturing process explains the differences better than the front-of-pack name.

faq.question: How much protein is in quark?
faq.answer: Many quark products provide roughly 10–13 g per 100 g, although moisture, fat, and processing can move the number. Check the specific label.

faq.question: Is quark the same as skyr?
faq.answer: No. They can overlap in protein and texture, but quark is traditionally an acid-set fresh cheese while skyr has its own cultured and concentrated production process.

faq.question: What is the difference between quark and cottage cheese?
faq.answer: Quark is smooth and homogeneous, while cottage cheese retains visible curds. Their protein contents can overlap, but texture, sodium, and processing are usually different.
